controls.text: Every one of the 1,055 checks was refused outright by the host.
controls.label: unsupported
controls.reason: Only 341 of 1,055 findings are access denials; the rest are absences, failed tests, other errors, and passes.

controls.text: A machine reaches all 29 of the resources that agencies publish for it from the data page.
controls.label: unsupported
controls.reason: 15 of the 29 pairs where the object exists are not reachable from the product page, so a machine does not reach all 29.

controls.text: The Census Bureau passes every one of its 39 published rows.
controls.label: unsupported
controls.reason: CENSUS has 18 failing of 39 judged rows, so it does not pass every one.

reals.text: This measurement covers all 16 federal statistical agencies.
reals.label: supported
reals.reason: 16 statistical bodies are on the cycle, which is what 'all 16 federal statistical agencies' means by the glossary.

reals.text: A plain, identified machine client is frequently refused before it can read anything, and much of what it looks for is not served at all.
reals.label: supported
reals.reason: The client is one identified, unauthenticated client; 341 of 1,055 findings are access denials and 415 are absences, which supports 'frequently refused' and 'much is not served'.

reals.text: Resources that agencies do publish often cannot be reached by a machine that starts at the data page.
reals.label: supported
reals.reason: 15 of 29 pairs (and 54 of 88 per page) exist but no product page reaches them, which supports 'often'.

answers.q1: (a) No. Page 1 supports 'complex' (SI readiness runs across data publishing, web practice, metadata standards and policy at once), 'beyond any one expert' (no one person holds all of it) and 'we meet an SI problem with SI', but nothing on the page says SI readiness is fast-moving; the only change noted is that people increasingly reach statistics through SI systems, which is about adoption, not about the readiness problem moving fast. (b) Yes: a decision support system that measures what a machine actually meets on the site rather than what the agency says, maps each result onto a readiness framework and one standard scale, and says what to fix first for the best value. (c) Yes: an executive, a site administrator, a data producer or anyone in the data's life can ask it questions, get answers at their own level, and the answers come with their sources attached. (d) No. Page 1 says the measurement covers all 16 federal statistical agencies and that the grid is the public tier, so 'ran the public tier on all 16' can be said, but 'standout results' cannot: the page reports only general findings (a plain identified machine client is frequently refused, much of what it looks for is not served, published resources often cannot be reached from the data page) and names no standout agency or result. Cannot be said: (a) and (d).

'USAFacts' and 'the four qualities USAFacts set out': who USAFacts is and why their qualities anchor the framework is not said. 3. 'with three more added': the three added qualities are never named. 4. 'knowledge graph': not explained. 5. 'A plain, identified machine client': what plain and identified mean for a client is not explained. 6. 'a machine that starts at the data page': which page is the data page is not defined. 7. 'When a source is overtaken': the meaning (superseded? out of date?) is not stated. 8. 'an agency-enabled tier that needs an agency to turn something on': the 'something' is never said. 9. 'a paid-tool tier': which tools, and who pays, is not said. 10. 'a rated judgment under a stated rubric': the rubric is referred to as stated but is not stated anywhere in the summary.
answers.q3: 1. That readiness is judged where the public and its tools actually meet the data: said in 'What we built' (measures what a machine actually meets, not what the agency says), again in the tiers section (the public tier is what any such system and any member of the public meets), and a third time in 'One caution' (we design around what the public can actually reach; readiness is judged where real users and their tools meet the data). 2. That no single person can hold every field involved: 'no one person holds all of it' in the opening, then 'no one need be expert in every field it touches' under who can use it. 3. That the tiers are divided by who can run them: in the section heading and again in the section's first sentence. 4. That the measurement covers all 16 federal statistical agencies: on page 1 under findings and again in the page 2 footnote (all sixteen, October 2026). 5. The date: 'Prepared 15 October 2026' at the top and 'in October 2026' in the footnote. 6. That the grid is the public tier, agency by agency: at the end of the tiers section on page 1 and in the page 2 heading. 7. The pass, partial and fail definitions: in the key above the grid and again in the footnote below it. 8. The fix-ordering idea: 'what to fix first for the best value' and 'the cheap high-value fixes before the larger ones' say the same thing in one sentence. 9. That answers carry sources: 'with their sources attached' and 'rather than off the cuff' make one point.
answers.q4: 1. 'rather than off the cuff' (already covered by 'with their sources attached'). 2. 'the cheap high-value fixes before the larger ones' (restates 'what to fix first for the best value'). 3. 'not only the largest commercial crawlers' (aside that adds nothing to the public-tier point). 4. 'so no one need be expert in every field it touches' (already said in the opening). 5. Either 'Prepared 15 October 2026' or the footnote's 'in October 2026'; one date suffices. 6. The page 1 sentence 'The grid on the next page is the public tier, agency by agency' (the page 2 heading says it). 7. The footnote's restatement of pass, fail and partial (the key already defines them); keep only the new content there, the handling of denials, unconfirmable absences and server errors, and the one-page rule. 8. The duplicated 'by who can run them' in either the heading or the first sentence of the tiers section. 9. 'a data producer or anyone working in the data's life' can shrink to one phrase; the list of roles is longer than the point needs. 10. Borderline: the sentence on overtaken sources being kept as history but no longer shaping advice is a product detail below the level of an executive summary, though it does support the trust claim.
answers.q5: Page 1: SI (also SI readiness, SI system); USAFacts; knowledge graph; plain, identified machine client; the data page; overtaken (as applied to a source); agency-enabled tier; paid-tool tier. Page 2 grid: the data is listed for discovery (what listing for discovery means, and the discovery file it implies); structured markup; a machine first entry point; data tools answer a machine; listed in a public inventory (which public inventory). The grid headings 'machine format', 'documented machine interface', 'full dataset download', 'crawlers allowed', 'machine readable release date / licence / change history' and 'methodology in reachable structured text' are plain enough for a CIO to follow, and the key symbols are defined, so they are not listed.

Page 2 grid and fixes: 'product' and 'product page' (used throughout for a statistical dataset or publication without being introduced); 'serve it with its own media type' (the MIME-type concept under an unfamiliar name); 'a documented machine interface' (a circumlocution for API that is never tied to the word); 'robots.txt' (a web-specific file not explained); 'the discovery file that is already served' and 'listed for discovery' (the file, presumably a sitemap, is never named); 'structured markup' and 'type the product page's existing markup as a dataset' (schema.org-style typing, unexplained); 'a machine first entry point' and 'machine-first entry point' (undefined, and the fix merely repeats the check); 'data tools answer a machine' together with its fix 'return a real status for routes that do not exist' ('routes' and 'real status' are HTTP jargon, and the fix does not obviously match the check name); 'methodology in reachable structured text' ('structured text' undefined); 'machine readable licence'; 'public data inventory' (a specific federal artefact, not explained); 'machine readable change history' versus the fix's 'version history' (two names for one thing); 'unconfirmable absence' in the closing paragraph; and the pass/partial/fail symbols rest on 'data pages', which is never defined.
